claim: Token-level sparse attention's indexer must score every historical key for every query, making per-layer indexing cost O(L^2) — the same asymptotic scaling as dense attention — so the indexer becomes the dominant cost at long context.
stance_target: The repo's claim that CSA2's indexer is a second attention running in parallel whose overhead can erase the sparsity win
scope_conditions: DSA-style token-level sparse attention (DeepSeek-V3.2, GLM-5); indexer runs once per query per layer
quoted_support: if the prefix length is L and the indexer runs once per query per layer, the per-layer indexing cost is O(L2)—the same asymptotic scaling as dense attention. As context lengths push toward 128K or 1M tokens, the indexer can transition from a negligible overhead into the dominant cost component.

claim: Measured at 64K context with top-k=2048, the Sparse MLA operator costs a roughly constant ~1.6 ms while the DSA indexer reaches 5.6 ms, so the indexer is ~3.5x the sparse-attention cost and is the main bottleneck.
stance_target: The repo's claim that the indexer, not the sparse attention, is what CSA2 must pay for
scope_conditions: NVIDIA A100, TileLang kernels for both indexers, query len 1024, final top-k 2048, block size B=128
quoted_support: With 2048 selected tokens, the Sparse MLA operator consistently costs about 1.6 ms, while the indexer reaches 5.6 ms at 64K context length. This suggests that the main performance bottleneck in DSA lies in the indexer rather than in Sparse MLA itself.

claim: HISA replaces the flat token scan with two stages — mean-pooled block representatives scored for coarse filtering, then the original DSA indexer applied only within the retained blocks — preserving the token-level top-k interface and the KV cache layout.
stance_target: The repo's description of CSA2's hierarchical sparse indexer as a pooled-block candidate-pool cap
scope_conditions: Block partitioning M = ceil(L/B); pooled key k_b = Pool({k_s | s in B_b}); top-m blocks then top-k tokens
quoted_support: a block-level coarse filtering stage that scores pooled block representations to discard irrelevant regions, followed by (2) a token-level refinement stage that applies the original indexer exclusively within the retained candidate blocks.

claim: HISA's per-query indexing cost is O(L/B + mB) rather than O(L), subject to the feasibility constraint mB >= k.
stance_target: The claim that a candidate-pool cap converts the indexer's quadratic scan into a bounded one
scope_conditions: Pooled representative keys maintained incrementally alongside the KV cache
quoted_support: the per-query indexing cost of HISA consists of scoring ceil(L/B) block representatives (Stage 1) and scoring at most mB candidate tokens (Stage 2): O(L/B + mB).

claim: HISA has three boundary regimes: when t <= k it is equivalent to dense attention; when k < t <= mB the coarse filter selects all blocks and it is equivalent to the original DSA indexer with no hierarchical advantage; only when t > mB does non-trivial block pruning activate.
stance_target: The repo's claim that at 32k the candidate-pool cap limits how much CSA2 can win relative to the published 1M-context numbers
scope_conditions: Effective prefix length t, candidate capacity mB, budget k
quoted_support: When t <= k, all prefix tokens are selected and HISA is equivalent to dense attention. When k < t <= mB, the coarse filter selects all blocks (since m >= M), and Stage 2 reduces the set to k tokens. HISA is equivalent to the original DSA indexer. When t > mB, the coarse filter performs non-trivial block pruning.

claim: With the paper's configuration (B=128, m=64, so mB=8192) a 32k prefix exceeds the candidate capacity by 4x and pruning is active; with the 16,384 cap the repo attributes to CSA2, 32k still exceeds it by 2x, so the cap does bind at 32k.
stance_target: The repo's phrasing that CSA2's 16,384 candidate cap 'barely binds' at 32k — it binds by a factor of two
scope_conditions: Arithmetic from HISA's boundary condition t > mB; B=128, m=64 gives mB=8192; CSA2 cap taken as 16,384
quoted_support: When t > mB, the coarse filter performs non-trivial block pruning, activating HISA's hierarchical advantage, which becomes increasingly pronounced as the sequence length grows.

claim: At 64K context HISA delivers ~2.16x indexer speedup at a 4:1 first-stage compression ratio (16K candidate budget) and up to 3.75x under a fixed 8K budget; the abstract cites 2-4x kernel-level speedup at 64K.
stance_target: The magnitude of the hierarchical-indexer win at long context, which the run must scale down for 32k
scope_conditions: NVIDIA A100, TileLang kernels, query len 1024, top-k 2048, B=128
quoted_support: At 64K context length, HISA delivers an approximately 2.16x speedup with a 4:1 first-stage compression ratio (corresponding to a 16K candidate budget), and up to 3.75x speedup under a fixed 8K budget.

claim: HISA is training-free: it is applied at inference time by replacing the indexer module, with no fine-tuning and no architectural modification.
stance_target: The repo's claim that CSA2's hierarchical indexer adds 'extra code and an extra loss term' to training — the hierarchical stage adds zero training cost
scope_conditions: DeepSeek-V3.2 and GLM-5, indexer replaced at inference; NIAH and LongBench run without additional training
quoted_support: Both HISA and Block-Sparse are training-free: they are applied at inference time by replacing the indexer module, with no fine-tuning or architectural modification.

claim: End-to-end in SGLang on DeepSeek-V3.2 (8xH200, TP=8, 128K input / 512 output), HISA reaches 9712.21 tok/s vs DSA's 5868.43, TTFT 62722.91 ms vs 106449.81 ms and TPOT 46.96 ms vs 73.02 ms — 1.65x throughput, 1.70x TTFT, 1.55x TPOT.
stance_target: The claim that hierarchical indexing converts into real serving throughput, not just kernel microbenchmarks
scope_conditions: SGLang, DeepSeek-V3.2, 8xH200 TP=8, 128K input, 512 output tokens per request, 10 random requests; HISA operators in TileLang/Triton vs DeepSeek's hand-tuned CUDA
quoted_support: HISA achieves 1.65x throughput and 1.70x TTFT speedup despite its TileLang/Triton operators being less mature than the official DSA baseline's hand-tuned CUDA kernels

claim: HISA closely matches DSA on Needle-in-a-Haystack across 8K-648K contexts and 0-100% needle depth, with only marginal degradation at extreme lengths and depths, while the block-sparse baseline degrades badly in the middle of the context.
stance_target: Whether hierarchical selection preserves quality without retraining
scope_conditions: DeepSeek-V3.2, HISA 4:1 ratio and block indexer, no additional training; NIAH 8K-648K
quoted_support: The original DSA achieves near-perfect retrieval across all context lengths and needle positions. HISA closely matches this performance, with only marginal degradation at extreme lengths and depths

claim: LongBench averages: DeepSeek-V3.2 DSA 51.05 vs HISA 50.78 (-0.27) vs Block-Sparse 49.54; GLM-5 DSA 46.01 vs HISA 46.32 (+0.31) vs Block-Sparse 42.67 — so hierarchical indexing costs about 0.3 points and clearly beats block-only selection.
stance_target: The quality cost of replacing the flat indexer with a hierarchical one
scope_conditions: LongBench via lm-eval, DeepSeek-V3.2 and GLM-5, all sparse methods applied at inference time without training
quoted_support: Without additional training, it closely matches DSA on LongBench and substantially outperforms the corresponding block-sparse baseline on NIAH.

claim: HISA's indexer kernels are TileLang and were benchmarked on an NVIDIA A100 (SM80), the same architecture class as the CMP 170HX's GA100, so the dominant cost component of DSA has an SM80-runnable implementation even though the cuDNN DSA kernels are SM90/SM100-only.
stance_target: The repo's premise that no DSA path runs on SM80 — the indexer does, via TileLang on A100
scope_conditions: Kernel-level microbenchmarks, both indexers in TileLang; HISA retains the official flashmla sparse path downstream, which is Hopper-oriented
quoted_support: Both implementations use TileLang kernels, with DSA following the official reference implementation. ... All comparisons are conducted on an NVIDIA A100 GPU.

claim: The authors name 'training-aware HISA' — jointly training the block-scoring stage — as an open direction they have NOT pursued, so the coarse filter is currently untrained and its accuracy is bounded by mean pooling.
stance_target: Whether the hierarchical stage could be trained on the box, and what that would cost
scope_conditions: Future-work section; current block stage represents each block with a single pooled vector
quoted_support: Training-aware HISA: while HISA currently operates as a training-free inference-time replacement, jointly training the block scoring stage may improve the coarse filter's accuracy, particularly for such boundary cases.

claim: Mean pooling a block into a single representative vector can fail when a block crosses a semantic boundary, so the coarse filter can discard blocks containing the target information; proposed mitigations are overlapping blocks, adaptive boundaries or max pooling.
stance_target: The information-loss risk of a pooled-block candidate cap
scope_conditions: Future-work section; NIAH shows marginal degradation at extreme lengths and depths
quoted_support: the current block-level stage represents each block with a single pooled vector, which can fail when a block crosses a semantic boundary and the pooled representation does not reflect the most important token.

claim: HISA forces the first and last blocks into the selected set, following MoBA, because they contain the attention sink and local context — a detail any box-side reimplementation must preserve to keep quality.
stance_target: The implementation contract for a CSA2-style indexer on this box
scope_conditions: Stage 1 block selection; also simplifies boundary handling for packed sequences of varying lengths
quoted_support: Following MoBA, the first and the last blocks are always included in Ct, as they contain the attention sink and local contexts.
